questions.prompt: How would you prove that renaming title to displayTitle kept records already saved by the old app?
questions.scenario: V2 Draft renames title to displayTitle and adds a required origin. The new app opens a fresh database, but no saved V1 store has been tested.
questions.androidBridge: Use Room migration testing as a preservation analogy. Core Data maps managed object models and owns its private SQLite schema; it is not a place to copy raw Room SQL.
rubric: Saves a real V1 SQLite store with the historical model before opening it with V2.
Keeps the old model available and defines the rename identity and historical default.
Checks each account, ID, title and origin rather than only row count or successful construction.
Separates mapping inference and model discovery from current CRUD and JSON upgrades.
Reports the actual toolchain and runtime checks and leaves unrun device or cutover checks pending.
questions.answerHTML:
Make a real V1 SQLite store first. Save two accounts with the same record ID but different titles on the context queue, then close the writer. This checks both text preservation and account separation. That establishes historical persisted data rather than reconstructing current-model objects. V2 gives displayTitle the old canonical rename identity, through renamingIdentifier, and gives origin a meaningful historical default. I would retain both model versions and either use supported automatic inference or explicitly obtain a mapping and migrate into a separate candidate.

After opening that candidate with V2, I would compare the full account, ID, title and origin values with the expected records. Equal counts could hide lost text or cross-account replacement. I would also reopen the preserved source with V1 and inject unsupported-source and destination-failure cases.

A JSON decoder version test verifies another format, and an in-memory CRUD test skips SQLite compatibility. The evidence must name the actual store, toolchain and assertions. Accepting the candidate is separate from switching the app to it. Cutover needs contexts to stop using the old store, replacement that handles SQLite sidecar files and a compatible recovery path.
followUps: Which rename identity must V3 keep if displayTitle is renamed again?
How would you test a relationship or uniqueness change that cannot use an inferred mapping?
pitfalls: Calling an in-memory insert with the current model a migration test.
Treating a successful open or equal row count as proof that all records were preserved.

questions.prompt: How would you recover when an upgrade cannot open some installed stores while preserving local drafts?
questions.scenario: The release encounters unsupported metadata, corrupt bytes and destination I/O failures. A legacy cache helper deletes and retries; the rollout owner proposes using that policy for drafts.
questions.androidBridge: Room destructive fallback is similarly a data-policy decision. The recovery mechanics differ for Core Data coordinators, model bundles and SQLite sidecars.
rubric: Separates unsupported format, corruption, temporary unavailability, packaging and destination failures.
Preserves irreplaceable source data and isolates any partial candidate.
Names cutover and rollback owners and a source-compatible restore or forward repair.
Defines preservation fixtures, rollout stop conditions and privacy-safe diagnostics.
Explains why a legacy cache-deletion branch does not make durable drafts disposable.
questions.answerHTML:
Decide what the data means before choosing recovery. An unsent draft may exist nowhere else. A cache that can be downloaded again has a different loss policy. Unsupported metadata can be valid data a newer binary understands; corruption and access unavailability need different responses. The legacy branch is evidence of an existing policy, not authorization to erase new durable intent.

The migration owner should preserve the source, produce a distinct candidate, validate domain projections, and switch stores only after stopping old access, performing a supported replacement and reopening the candidate. Partial candidates are diagnostic artifacts under a bounded retention/protection policy. Missing packaged models should stop rollout as a build defect rather than trigger data reset.

Test saved old stores from every supported version. Also control failures for corrupt data, unsupported versions and writes to the destination. Stop rollout when preservation fails or classification is unknown. A rollback binary may not understand V2, so recovery needs a retained compatible source or forward repair; source rollback alone is insufficient. Diagnostics expose schema/error categories and synthetic evidence, not user draft contents.
followUps: Who stops or coordinates an extension still using the old store during cutover?
What recovery remains if the newer binary already saved V2 data?
pitfalls: Erasing failed stores to make launch-success metrics look better.
Expecting the previous binary to reverse schema changes merely by being reinstalled.

questions.prompt: The server applied an edit, but its reply was lost. What must the outbox save so restart can recover without duplicating the edit?
questions.scenario: The synthetic server changed a title. The client never received acknowledgment and exits with that operation still pending.
questions.androidBridge: Room plus WorkManager can provide local persistence and scheduling, but neither supplies remote idempotency. iOS scheduling grants are different; the queue must survive independently.
rubric: Commits the local edit and pending command in one durable boundary.
Keeps account scope, immutable payload, operation ID and precondition across restart.
Requires a documented server contract that commits the effect and receipt atomically.
Keeps ambiguous intent until the local acknowledgment is durably saved.
Separates ordinary restart checks from abrupt crash, power-loss and real-service evidence.
Resolves the whole dependent record lane atomically, or rejects multiple pending edits to that record.
questions.answerHTML:
An outbox is a saved list of commands waiting for delivery. Each command needs a stable operation ID, unchanged payload, account, ordering and precondition information, and delivery state. The local edit and command must be committed together, or process death can leave an edit with no future transmission. The operation ID remains stable across replay and credential refresh.

A lost reply is like losing a receipt after paying: the payment may already have happened. A timeout does not prove the server rejected the command. I would retain the command and replay only under a verified service contract that binds identity to payload and account. The server must persist its effect and receipt atomically; local UUID generation cannot manufacture exactly-once semantics. The original receipt must remain usable for the supported replay window.

After restart, select and authenticate the account, rotate the session’s ownership token, reload the command and reconcile its receipt. If saving acknowledgment fails, keep the command and reconcile again. A deterministic separate-process fixture can prove ordinary exit/reload and one synthetic effect. It does not establish receipt expiry behavior, sudden power-loss durability or production endpoint support.

Giving a replacement a fresh ID does not fix its position in the intent sequence. Either reconcile the entire record’s dependent command lane and preconditions atomically, or support only one pending command per record and replace it in its original slot. Reject unsupported dependencies without changing the persisted queue.
followUps: How should recovery change if the service’s replay receipt has expired?
What stays pending if acknowledgment arrives but saving local removal fails?
pitfalls: Generating a new operation ID for each retry of the same intent.
Treating cancellation as proof that the server had no effect.
Appending a conflict replacement after dependent edits without reconciling their preconditions.

questions.prompt: How could a deleted record reappear after an old offline update? Define a bounded stale-write prevention and conflict-resolution policy.
questions.scenario: An older update waits behind a delete. The client immediately hides the row, and the proposed server delete also removes all revision history.
questions.androidBridge: A Room row deletion is not a remote tombstone protocol. Kotlin coroutine ordering or a WorkManager retry policy cannot resolve stale service intent.
rubric: Keeps durable delete intent after hiding or removing the local row.
Keeps a revision-bearing tombstone or another reviewed stale-write prevention contract.
Orders dependent commands and pauses conflicts instead of silently overwriting.
Gives an explicitly rebased or recreated intent a new ID and current precondition.
Checks the account epoch before local acknowledgment and names remaining retention and concurrency work.
Reconciles the entire dependent record lane atomically, or rejects multiple pending edits to that record.
questions.answerHTML:
Hiding the row does not mean its delete has reached the server. Keep the saved delete command. If the server forgets the latest revision too, an old update can look like a new create. The deleted record can then reappear. A tombstone is a retained marker of deletion with the revision needed to reject that old write. I would retain a revision-bearing tombstone or use another explicit server policy that rejects stale intent during the supported offline window.

This bounded fixture processes one account’s commands in first-in, first-out order and pauses when a conflict appears. That sacrifices throughput for reviewable ordering. Per-record lanes are an alternative only after delete/recreate dependencies and concurrent acknowledgments are specified. A revision mismatch is retained for user/domain resolution rather than retried forever.

Deliberately recreating the record or rebasing an edit onto the current revision is new intent: it receives a fresh operation ID and a current precondition. Reusing the conflicted ID with changed payload violates idempotency. I would test delete persistence through reload, stale update rejection and A-to-B-to-A before acknowledgment. The late effect may already exist remotely, but its old ticket cannot commit locally. Tombstone retention, server authorization and cross-device merge remain independently owned contracts.

A new operation ID alone does not preserve the order of dependent intent. Either reconcile the entire record’s dependent command lane and preconditions atomically, or support only one pending command per record and replace it in its original slot. Reject unsupported dependencies without changing the persisted queue.
followUps: How would independent record lanes change throughput and which failures block later work?
What agreed offline window and server policy would allow a tombstone to be removed?
pitfalls: Dropping the delete command when the local row disappears.
Choosing last-write-wins without reviewing deletion semantics and authorization.
Appending a conflict replacement after dependent edits without reconciling their preconditions.

questions.prompt: How do state, PKCE and the current account attempt control whether a callback may install credentials?
questions.scenario: A mock provider returns a valid authorization code while a second login attempt starts. Both callback URLs are well formed.
questions.androidBridge: External browser flows resemble Android Custom Tabs conceptually. Apple presentation/callback ownership and Keychain policies require their own APIs; neither platform's callback alone proves resource authorization.
rubric: Checks the exact callback destination and rejects missing or duplicate state and code fields.
Separates state’s attempt matching from PKCE’s code-redemption proof.
Consumes the callback once and validates the verifier and challenge at the provider.
Rechecks epoch after exchange and publishes only after the vault save succeeds.
Names fixed test entropy, the synthetic provider and real browser and security behavior still unverified.
questions.answerHTML:
State labels the login attempt so its callback can be matched. PKCE, Proof Key for Code Exchange, separately requires the code exchange to prove knowledge of the verifier behind the authorization challenge. I would validate the exact callback destination and reject missing, wrong or duplicate state and code values. A correct-looking URL is not sufficient.

Accept the matching callback once. Then exchange its code using that attempt’s verifier. The mock provider checks S256 and consumes the code once. The fixed verifier demonstrates encoding against a reference vector; it is not production entropy or a complete provider implementation.

The exchange may suspend. A newer login or logout can take ownership while the old exchange still succeeds. Success alone does not grant permission to install its credentials. Credential installation must check the captured epoch at the final owner and save the vault before publishing a durable session. A storage failure stays distinct from denial or user cancellation. I would order a late-result test explicitly. Browser presentation, random generation, redirect registration, identity verification and server authorization need separate platform/provider evidence.
followUps: Why must duplicate state fields be rejected even if one matches?
Where would a server-verified passkey result enter the same account-ownership checks?
pitfalls: Expecting PKCE to replace state and exact redirect validation.
Installing credentials after exchange succeeds without checking the current epoch.

questions.prompt: Refresh consumed the old token, but saving the new credential failed. How would you recover without assuming the old token can be retried?
questions.scenario: The synthetic provider rotates the refresh token and consumes the old one. FakeVault.save throws locked. The old credential view remains, and another caller wants to retry refresh.
questions.androidBridge: A synchronized Kotlin repository can serialize refresh callers but cannot undo server rotation. Keychain and Android key storage also have different locked-state and restoration policies.
rubric: Identifies remote success followed by local failure across separate boundaries.
Rejects retrying the old token without provider-supported reconciliation or grace.
Defines one shared refresh owner and separates waiter cancellation from logout.
Closes local authorization on logout and keeps failed cleanup obligations.
States limits of fake-vault, durable sign-out, actual Keychain and real-provider evidence.
questions.answerHTML:
The old credential still appearing in memory does not make its refresh token valid. The server consumed that token during rotation, but the vault failed to save its replacement. In this mock, an unlocked retry is denied because there is no reconciliation endpoint or rotation grace rule. The checked recovery is explicit reauthentication. A real integration may use provider-documented reconciliation, but cannot infer replay safety from a transport or storage error.

Let the account service own one refresh operation shared by callers. Canceling one caller’s wait should not automatically cancel other waiters or log out the account. The compact fixture is single-caller and does not verify coalescing. Logout invalidates ownership and closes local authorization even if credential deletion fails.

Save a properly protected sign-out or cleanup obligation. On restart, check it before restoring any credential that survived in the vault. Classify interaction restrictions separately from item absence and configuration errors. Verification should include late refresh completion, post-rotation storage failure, denied retry and recovery. Fake-vault checks establish state decisions; signed Keychain availability, durable sign-out and real provider rotation semantics remain separate work.
followUps: What should canceling one waiter do to the other callers sharing refresh?
What recovery is required if logout also fails to save its durable sign-out marker?
pitfalls: Assuming unlocking the vault makes a consumed token safe to replay.
Expecting actor isolation to merge refresh requests automatically across await.

questions.prompt: Where must the final account-epoch check run when saving a prepared snapshot to Core Data?
questions.scenario: An actor checks the account, then awaits privateContext.perform. Logout is queued before that closure runs. The developer claims the earlier check is sufficient.
questions.androidBridge: A Kotlin Mutex around repository state does not protect an independently queued Room transaction after the lock is released. Core Data additionally has context-queue confinement.
rubric: Explains the gap between the earlier check and the queued transaction.
Orders account reset and mutation through the actual transaction owner.
Checks epoch before mutation without a suspension that can change ownership before save.
Keeps managed objects on their context queue and transfers snapshots or IDs.
Explains whole dedicated-context rollback and the limits of the MainActor-to-main-queue bridge.
questions.answerHTML:
Check the epoch where account reset and the actual fetch, change and save are ordered together. An epoch is a session generation; account A returning later does not make an old A generation current. Checking on an actor and then awaiting another queue leaves a window in which logout can win. A queued closure must validate the captured account and epoch before touching managed state.

The lab gives a dedicated main-queue writer a MainActor owner. That specific setup establishes its bridge; it is not an assumption valid for any context. It resets and rotates epoch during activation, enters performAndWait for mutation, and asserts the established MainActor bridge inside the Sendable closure. No await separates the guard from save. A private context would need its own serialized command owner, not the same assumption.

Transfer prepared values as Sendable snapshots. Sendable concerns safe transfer of these values; awaiting the context operation separately permits suspension. Managed objects stay inside the context queue, and failed saves roll back the dedicated writer's whole pending scope. That design would be wrong if unrelated UI edits shared the context. I would test A-to-B-to-A with an old epoch and read through a fresh context after a valid commit, keeping in-memory host evidence separate from disk restart and device protection.
followUps: Why is MainActor.assumeIsolated not justified in an arbitrary private context closure?
Which parent and store saves would be needed if this were a child context?
pitfalls: Treating actor isolation as a replacement for Core Data context confinement.
Calling whole-context rollback a harmless undo of only one row.

questions.prompt: How should startup behave when protected files cannot open and an earlier logout left cleanup unfinished?
questions.scenario: A background launch finds an account label in its journal, possibly surviving credential material and a protected store that is currently unavailable.
questions.androidBridge: Android Direct Boot offers a familiar availability question, but iOS file protection and Keychain classes are distinct policies rather than direct equivalents of Android storage directories.
rubric: Separates a selected account label from usable authorization and accessible storage.
Resolves durable sign-out obligations before restoring credentials.
Defers protected access without replacing saved intent with an empty store.
Explains retained open handles versus new opens under completeUnlessOpen.
Names bootstrap and cleanup owners and distinguishes injected host failures from device evidence.
questions.answerHTML:
An account label says which account was selected. It does not prove usable authorization. A credential left behind by failed cleanup is not enough either. Bootstrap first resolves durable sign-out and cleanup obligations, then establishes credential availability and selected-account policy. Only afterward can it inspect store compatibility, restore account-scoped intent and grant replay.

If protected data is unavailable, say the work is deferred until access is possible. It must not be converted to an empty store or trigger migration deletion. The completeUnlessOpen protection class can preserve access through an already open handle. It does not guarantee that a new read or a database sidecar file can open while the device is locked. Availability notifications can schedule bounded retry; actual I/O still decides the outcome.

One owner coordinates the UI, vault cleanup, durable marker and store access. Classify each resource’s failures: these operations do not form one shared transaction. If marker writing fails, withhold automatic credential restoration until explicit reconciliation. I would require injected no-write tests, account-ordering tests and a passcode-enabled scratch-device matrix. Host success and iOS type-checking do not establish locked-device, Keychain or sudden-process-death behavior.
followUps: What recovery applies if file bytes were replaced but backup-exclusion configuration failed?
Which device evidence would justify changing the credential’s Keychain accessibility class?
pitfalls: Treating temporarily unavailable protected data as proof that no account exists.
Assuming logout across vault, files and network is atomic.
